newsitem.title: USA: Group urges stricter limits on U.S. credit cards.
newsitem.headline: Group urges stricter limits on U.S. credit cards.

text.p: An influential consumer group on Tuesday urged credit card issuers to take steps to reduce debt levels, saying they were imposing a "crushing burden" on American households.

The Consumer Federation of America said a study it conducted showed tens of millions of households were saddled with significant credit card debt loads and that both consumers and card issuers bore responsibility.

"We don't object to any households holding credit cards," the group's executive director, Stephen Brobeck, said at a news conference. "It is how many credit cards are being issued and what the credit card limits are that are the issue."

The Consumer Federation's study estimated that in 1996, consumers charged more than $1 trillion on their credit cards. Of that, it estimated that nearly $400 billion of the charges were being "revolved," incurring interest.
It said that revolving consumer credit, which has been rising at double-digit rates for the past four years, averaged $6,000 to $7,000 for the roughly 60 million households that held it.

The Consumer Federation and another non-profit group, Bankcard Holders of America, are taking aim, in particular, at the marketing tactics of card issuers, such as aggressive mail and telephone solicitation campaigns and offers of rebates and shopping credits to entice borrowers.

"While consumers bear responsibility for the debts they incur, credit card issuers have been encouraging consumers to go deep in debt -- with marketing tactics that reward those who carry balances, and penalise those who pay in full," said Ruth Susswein, executive director of Bankcard Holders of America.
A major concern of both groups was the targeting of the marketing strategies toward those in the lower-middle income brackets.
The Consumer Federation proposed several steps for credit card companies to take, including showing more restraint in the number of cards they issue and the credit limits they allow.
The group suggested that in most cases, companies should not approve total credit lines that exceed 20 percent of a household's annual income.
The federation said it would ask major card companies to set such limits on their own and said legislative action should be considered only as a last resort.
Still, representatives of credit card issuers and the banking industry were quick to denounce the proposals as detrimental to consumers and the economy.

Thomas Layman, chief economist at Visa USA, said that while rising debt levels merit concern, consumers as a whole have benefited from a higher standard of living due to more widespread issuance of credit that has helped boost demand in the economy.
Jim Chessen, chief economist for the American Bankers Association, said suggestions of limiting the number of cards issued were "anti-consumer" and "anti-competitive."
Worries over mounting levels of consumer debt have been expressed by a number of lawmakers and bank regulators.

Many of those officials have said that while the situation bears watching, they did not see an imminent threat to the soundness of the banking system or the economy from the high consumer debt levels.
Nonetheless, an increase in personal bankruptcy filings has helped put a spotlight on the potential problems.
For their part, credit card issuers have suggested that Congress tighten bankruptcy laws, imposing greater restrictions on filings for debt foregiveness under the Chapter 7 bankruptcy protection law.
